name: Sudan
summary: A country on the middle Nile, independent from Anglo-Egyptian rule since 1956. Long civil wars led to the independence of South Sudan in 2011, and a new war began in 2023.

knownFor.label: Meroë pyramids
knownFor.note: Ancient Kushite pyramids, more numerous than Egypt’s.

knownFor.label: Gum arabic
knownFor.note: Sudan is the largest producer of this tree resin used in food.

knownFor.label: Confluence of the Niles
knownFor.note: The Blue and White Nile meet at Khartoum.

location.value: North Africa, with a Red Sea coast; about 1,886,000 km², Africa's third-largest country. It was Africa's largest country until South Sudan seceded in 2011.

terrain.value: Dry semi-desert in the centre and north (Nubian and Bayuda deserts), with grasslands and tropical savanna in the south.

climate.value: Very sunny; rainfall increases towards the south.

resources.value: Rich mineral resources, including gold, petroleum, copper and iron.

disasters.value: Devastating floods in 2007 affected over 400,000 people; desertification is a serious problem.

urbanisation.value: Khartoum is the capital and most populous city; Greater Khartoum (with Omdurman and Khartoum North) had about 5.2 million people.

disease.value: Malaria, cholera; disease spread during the wars.

migration.value: By the end of 2023, over 5.8 million people were internally displaced and more than 1.5 million had fled abroad as refugees.

economicBase.value: Mainly agriculture, because of sanctions, isolation and instability; gold production reached 82 tonnes in 2015.

tradeRoutes.value: Oil pipelines run to Port Sudan on the Red Sea coast.

wealth.value: A least developed country and among the poorest in the world; over 60% of people live in poverty.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the centre and the regions.

governmentType.value: Long periods of military rule, including Omar al-Bashir's military dictatorship (1989–2019); a transitional government after 2019, overthrown by a military coup in 2021.

keyRulers.value: Ismail al-Azhari (first prime minister). Gaafar Nimeiry. Omar al-Bashir (1989–2019).

institutions.value: Weak institutions; the army and paramilitary forces hold power.

stability.value: Very unstable: two north–south civil wars, conflict in Darfur from 2003, and a third civil war since 2023.

eliteConflict.value: Conflict between the army and the Rapid Support Forces since 2023.

armyAndTech.value: The Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

majorWars.value: A north–south civil war (1955–1972); the Second Sudanese Civil War, ended by a 2005 peace agreement; war in Darfur from 2003; a third civil war since 2023.

alliancesRivals.value: Shifting ties with Egypt, the Gulf states and Russia.

scienceEducation.value: Around 25–30 universities, teaching mainly in Arabic or English.

communicationTransport.value: Railways from colonial times; Nile boats; roads.

religion.value: After South Sudan split off in 2011, over 97% of people in Sudan were Muslim, mostly Sufi or Salafi.

languageWriting.value: Arabic and English have been the official languages since 2005; about 70 languages are native to Sudan.

socialStructure.value: Arab and non-Arab identities have been a source of conflict.

sharedIdentity.value: Divided by region, ethnicity and religion.

dailyLife.value: Mud-brick houses and round huts; sorghum porridge, beans (ful).

neighbours.value: Egypt, Libya, Chad, the Central African Republic, South Sudan, Ethiopia and Eritrea.

ideasReligions.value: Islamist rule began under Nimeiry; Bashir's government introduced an Islamic legal code nationwide in 1989.

peakPeriod.value: An oil-fuelled boom, with growth of about 9% in 2007.

declineSignals.value: Civil wars, coups and the loss of the south.

outcome.value: Still in existence, at war since 2023.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts documented; casualty and population figures disputed.
